title: Is It Possible to Make Smart Glasses That Aren’t Creepy?
gist: WIRED asks whether privacy-respecting smart glasses are possible and finds the answer is probably no: Meta has sold tens of millions of units and is selling better than ever despite users bypassing indicator lights and a face-recognition 'Name Tag' feature it only deleted after WIRED exposed it. An IDC analyst argues buyers want both privacy and normal-looking frames, so Consumer Reports is pushing California legislation mandating undefeatable recording indicators.

themes.theme: Smart-glasses gold rush and Meta's dominance

insights.claim: Companies of every size are piling into smart glasses, with Meta the largest player and the primary target of privacy criticism because its glasses capture images, audio and video of whatever the wearer looks at.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Meta owns both the category's installed base and its reputational risk — regulation aimed at the category is effectively regulation aimed at Meta.
insights.quote: Face computers are on the upswing, as companies, massive and tiny, are all vying for nuggets in the smart-glasses gold rush.
insights.locator: Face computers are on the upswing

insights.claim: Privacy controversy has not dented demand: Meta has sold tens of millions of smart-glasses units and the products are selling better than ever despite impassioned public debate.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Consumer backlash is not showing up in units — the privacy debate is a policy risk, not currently a demand risk, for Meta's hardware line.
insights.quote: Meta has sold tens of millions of units, and despite impassioned debates about privacy among tech watchdogs and the general public, the company’s glasses are selling better than ever.
insights.locator: As invasive as the technology can feel

insights.claim: Google and Samsung enter the smart-glasses market later this year and Apple is reportedly targeting 2027, having delayed production specifically to address privacy issues.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: The competitive window opens in 2026-2027; Apple delaying over privacy suggests it intends to compete on trust rather than on being first.
insights.quote: Apple is also reportedly working on smart glasses that could arrive in 2027, though it has reportedly delayed production to address the privacy issues.
insights.locator: This conversation around privacy and smart glasses is only going to grow

insights.claim: Genuine demand drivers exist beyond novelty, including quick photo capture, GoPro-style action video, and accessibility uses such as real-time captioning and Meta's Be My Eyes partnership for visually impaired users.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Accessibility is the use case that makes an outright ban politically untenable — it anchors the category's legitimacy against privacy pushback.
insights.locator: People have found genuinely useful reasons to wear the glasses

themes.theme: Meta's safeguards and the Name Tag reversal

insights.claim: Meta's recording indicator light has been defeated by users who figured out how to disable it, prompting the company to add anti-tamper features that shut the glasses down if they have been meddled with.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Hardware privacy signals are only as strong as their tamper resistance — the arms race Meta is now committing engineering resources to.
insights.quote: Meta’s smart glasses do have an indicator light to warn bystanders when they’re being recorded, though some Meta users have figured out how to bypass those safety features and disable the lights.
insights.locator: The prime target for such criticism is the biggest company in the space

insights.claim: Meta programmed an opt-in face-recognition feature called Name Tag into its smart glasses and only deleted the code from its app after a WIRED report exposed it, with CTO Andrew Bosworth subsequently confirming the feature's existence.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Face recognition on consumer eyewear was built and shelved rather than abandoned — journalism, not policy, was the binding constraint, and that constraint is reversible.
insights.quote: Earlier this year, Meta programmed a feature that, if enabled, would add face-recognition technology to its smart glasses. After a WIRED report exposed this feature, Meta then deleted the code from its app.
insights.locator: Other concerns about the glasses have continued to mount

insights.claim: Meta said at a June event that it is considering adding camera-free smart glasses to its lineup, implying it sees a real segment of buyers who want the form factor without the capture capability.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: A camera-free Meta SKU would validate privacy-first positioning and squeeze the small vendors currently differentiating on exactly that.
insights.locator: At an event in June, Meta also said

themes.theme: Privacy as a product differentiator for challengers

insights.claim: Smaller brands are courting the anti-Meta buyer with hardware-level privacy: Even Realities sells camera-free glasses as a deliberate differentiator and Solos ships frames with a pop-on privacy shield for the camera lenses.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Privacy is becoming a segmentation axis rather than a compliance checkbox — the niche where challengers can survive against Meta's scale.
insights.locator: Smaller brands have tried to appeal to the anti-Meta crowd

insights.claim: An enterprise optics executive frames the privacy debate itself as a bullish signal, arguing that the discussion only matters because the market is close to critical mass of products.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Industry insiders read controversy as adoption confirmation — a useful counter-indicator when privacy headlines are treated as a sector negative.
insights.quote: The fact that it's even a discussion point is really great for the industry
insights.locator: says Matt Margolis, vice president of business development at Vuzix

insights.claim: An IDC consumer-devices analyst argues truly private smart glasses are not achievable because the same buyers who want privacy also want glasses that look like normal glasses.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: The conflict is in consumer preference, not engineering — meaning no product fix resolves it and regulation becomes the only lever.
insights.quote: There is certainly a market incentive, right? People want this kind of thing, but at the same time, they also want glasses that look normal and look like regular glasses.
insights.locator: says Jitesh Ubrani, director of research on consumer devices

insights.claim: Making cameras conspicuous is a known design fix that the market has already rejected, as shown by Snapchat's bold early camera glasses and the ridicule of 2013 Google Glass wearers as 'Glassholes'.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Historical precedent says visible-camera designs fail commercially — so mandated visibility would be a real constraint on the category, not a costless fix.
insights.locator: But people don’t seem to want to wear obvious camera glasses

themes.theme: Why glasses differ from phone cameras

insights.claim: Smart glasses break the historical privacy bargain of phone cameras because a phone must be pulled out, held up and activated, while glasses record from a device designed to look innocuous.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Loss of the visible-capture signal is the specific harm regulators can target — expect rules written around notice and indicators rather than bans.
insights.quote: The fact that they are designed to be innocuous is the biggest difference
insights.locator: says Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist

insights.claim: Privacy advocates objected to cameras in smartphones and laptops before this, so the smart-glasses backlash follows a recognizable pattern of resistance that previous camera integrations ultimately overcame.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Historical base rate favors adoption winning out — but only after the notice conventions of each prior generation were settled.
insights.locator: Smart glasses are not even close to the first product

themes.theme: Policy response and broader surveillance backlash

insights.claim: Consumer Reports staff are backing California senate legislation that would require visible indicators on any device capable of recording audio or video and would prohibit users from disabling those indicators.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: A California indicator mandate would set the de facto national hardware spec for every camera-bearing wearable — the single most consequential rule pending for the category.
insights.locator: advocating for legislation in the California senate

insights.claim: The argument from Consumer Reports is that smart glasses need not be a privacy nightmare technically — social and economic incentives are what push them in that direction, which is why policy rather than product design must intervene.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Framing the problem as incentives-driven is what justifies mandates over voluntary standards — the intellectual basis of the coming rulemaking.
insights.quote: As technology develops and has the capacity to increasingly collect everything about all of us all the time, then that's where policy needs to come in

insights.claim: Smart-glasses pushback coincides with broader revolt against surveillance tech including Flock street cameras and the surveillance network at Madison Square Garden, with an EFF activist calling it the loudest, most pronounced pushback in years.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: A cross-category surveillance backlash raises the odds of broad legislation that catches facial recognition, ALPR and wearables together — a sector-wide policy risk.
insights.quote: All of this stuff this year has been a very loud, pronounced pushback in a way that I haven't seen in a while
insights.locator: The pushback against smart glasses comes at the same time
